newsitem.title: FRANCE: French growth seen speeding to 2.3 pct in 97-INSEE.
newsitem.headline: French growth seen speeding to 2.3 pct in 97-INSEE.

text.p: French national statistics institute INSEE forecast a pickup in economic growth to an annual 2.3 percent in 1997 from 1.5 percent in 1996.

Year-on-year growth was likely to show a steady acceleration, reaching 3.2 percent by year-end, compared with 2.4 percent at the end of the first half and 2.1 percent at the end of 1996, INSEE said in its latest economic outlook.
Stronger economic growth in 1997 is seen as vital to France's ability to curb its public deficit in order to meet conditions for taking part in European monetary union.
The stronger growth would take place against a backdrop of an increasingly favourable international environment, it said.
The industrial sector, helped by brisk foreign demand, competitiveness gains and firmer prices, would make a strong contribution to the acceleration.
"But even with job creation accelerating throughout the year, unemployment is not expected to do more than stabilise in the second half because of above-trend growth in the labour force," INSEE said.

Some 135,000 net new jobs were expected to be created in 1997 but this would be insufficient to make a dent in unemployment which would level off in the second half at its current level of around 12.5 percent, it forecast.
INSEE cautioned that maintenance of positive expectations on the part of business leaders was crucial to its growth and unemployment scenarios.
The previous conservative government forecast growth at a "minimum" 2.3 percent for 1997.

The external sector was believed to have made the strongest contribution to growth in the early part of the year before slowing down somewhat as the growth differential between France and its main trading partners gradually narrowed, INSEE said.

Demand from the corporate sector was seen taking up the baton in the second half through a reversal of the destocking process witnessed in the manufacturing sector and a gradual acceleration in investment.
Household consumption was expected to provide extra support for overall demand.
Net job creation was expected to accelerate as the year wore on, helped by improved expectations and accelerating growth.
There was clear improvement in the recruitment outlook in all sectors, according to latest surveys, INSEE said.
Services, especially temporary employment, were likely to remain the most dynamic area in terms of job creation despite a downward trend in the banking and insurance sector.
In building and public works, the rate of job losses, which was rapid in 1996, should slow down helped by a gradual improvement in the public works and residential housing fields.
Firms were likely to see a recovery in their operating earnings following a slight fall in 1996, INSEE said.

The nominal value of household incomes was set to rise this year, helped by a fall in income tax, although total wages and salaries received by households were likely to rise at about the same pace as in 1996.
The acceleration in income growth was likely to be more marked in real terms as a result of a slowdown in inflation.

The end of 1997 was expected to see year-on-year growth in spending power of around 2.4 percent compared with around 0.1 percent at end 1996. The increase on an annual average basis would be 1.6 percent.
